properties.name: Big Bone Lick
properties.title: Big Bone Lick
properties.subtitle: Boone County / salt lick & fossil beds
properties.history: Big Bone Lick was a mineral spring where Pleistocene mastodons, mammoths, and ground sloths left bones in the mud while seeking salt. Native peoples and later explorers—including Christopher Gist—collected fossils here; Thomas Jefferson later studied specimens from the lick. The site became Big Bone Lick State Historic Site, one of Kentucky’s earliest windows on deep time and a waypoint for salt hunters on the Ohio frontier.

properties.name: Lexington Named
properties.title: Lexington Named
properties.subtitle: Fayette County / McConnell Springs
properties.history: In early June 1775, William McConnell’s surveyors camped on a sinking spring of Elkhorn Creek when word arrived of the April 19 fight at Lexington, Massachusetts. They named the camp for that battle and returned east; permanent settlement waited until 1779, when Robert Patterson’s party built a blockhouse near present Main and Mill. Virginia established the town in 1782—the springs chose the site, the Revolution chose the name.

properties.name: Benjamin Logan / Logan's Station
properties.title: Benjamin Logan / Logan's Station
properties.subtitle: Lincoln County / St. Asaph near Stanford
properties.history: In 1775 Benjamin Logan left Boone's party and built Logan's Station (St. Asaph) near present-day Stanford—a stockade by Buffalo Spring that held through a roughly thirteen-day siege in May 1777. Logan hauled the wounded Burr Harrison inside under fire, then slipped out at night and walked about 150 miles to the Holston settlements for powder. He later helped write Kentucky's first constitution and settled on Bullskin Creek near Finchville in Shelby County.

properties.name: Shelbyville Founding
properties.title: Shelbyville Founding
properties.subtitle: Shelby County seat / Clear Creek
properties.history: Shelby County was carved from Jefferson County in 1792 and named for first governor Isaac Shelby. That October, at the first county court, Revolutionary veteran William Shannon donated about 50 acres on Clear Creek so the new seat would sit on the Frankfort-to-Falls road. Trustees required hewed-log houses with brick or stone chimneys; by 1800 the town had 262 people. Nearby Squire Boone's Painted Stone Station had been the earlier foothold—Shelbyville won the courthouse.

properties.name: Chickasaw / Jackson Purchase
properties.title: Chickasaw / Jackson Purchase
properties.subtitle: Western Kentucky / 1818 treaty
properties.history: West of the Tennessee River, Chickasaw hunting grounds stayed off Kentucky's settled map until October 19, 1818. Andrew Jackson and Isaac Shelby negotiated what became the Jackson Purchase: roughly 13,000 square miles (about 2,369 in Kentucky) for annuities. That treaty filled in the western counties from Ballard through McCracken and closed the last big Indigenous title claim inside the state.

properties.name: Frankfort Founding
properties.title: Frankfort Founding
properties.subtitle: Franklin County / Frank's Ford capital
properties.history: Before it was the capital, the site was a buffalo-trail ford on the Kentucky River. In 1780 pioneer Stephen Frank was killed in a skirmish there; settlers called the crossing Frank's Ford, which shortened to Frankfort. In 1786 Virginia chartered a town on land promoted by Gen. James Wilkinson. When Kentucky became a state in 1792, Frankfort outbid rivals for the capital, and Gideon Shryock's Greek Revival Old Capitol (1830) finally stuck after earlier buildings burned.

properties.name: Bullitt's Lick
properties.title: Bullitt's Lick
properties.subtitle: Bullitt County / Kentucky's first industry
properties.history: Salt was frontier white gold, and the only large commercial saltworks west of the Alleghenies during the Revolution sat about three miles west of present-day Shepherdsville. Capt. Thomas Bullitt surveyed the Salt River lick in 1773; production started in 1779 as workers boiled brine in rows of iron kettles. Pack trains and flatboats carried the salt across Kentucky, a fort went up in 1780, and a boomtown nicknamed Saltburg grew around the furnaces until cheaper salt arrived around 1830.

properties.name: George Rogers Clark / Corn Island
properties.title: George Rogers Clark / Corn Island
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County / Falls of the Ohio
properties.history: Virginia surveyor-turned-militia leader George Rogers Clark staged at Corn Island in the Falls of the Ohio in 1778, then launched the Illinois Campaign that took Kaskaskia and Vincennes from the British. The settlement he left behind became Louisville, chartered in 1780 and named for France’s Louis XVI. Fort Nelson later rose on the mainland as his western headquarters.

properties.name: Battle of Blue Licks
properties.title: Battle of Blue Licks
properties.subtitle: Robertson County / 1782 battlefield
properties.history: On August 19, 1782, about 182 Kentucky militia chasing Captain William Caldwell’s raiders walked into an ambush on a Licking River ridge in today’s Robertson County. Roughly 50 Butler’s Rangers and 200–300 Shawnee, Delaware, and Wyandot warriors fired from ravines and bluffs; Todd, Trigg, and Boone’s son Israel were among the dead. It was the settlers’ bloodiest Revolutionary defeat in Kentucky, months after Yorktown.

properties.name: Great Saltpetre Cave
properties.title: Great Saltpetre Cave
properties.subtitle: Rockcastle County / War of 1812 powder
properties.history: South of Mount Vernon in Rockcastle County, Great Saltpetre Cave was mined hard for calcium nitrate during the War of 1812, when British blockades cut off imported saltpeter for gunpowder. Dozens of workers (many enslaved) leached cave earth in wooden vats and shipped crystals to powder mills until trade reopened after 1815. The Rockcastle Karst Conservancy keeps the preserve today.

properties.name: Richard Henderson / Transylvania
properties.title: Richard Henderson / Transylvania
properties.subtitle: Henderson County / Transylvania Company
properties.history: North Carolina judge Richard Henderson reorganized his investors as the Transylvania Company in early 1775, then bargained at Sycamore Shoals for roughly 20 million acres between the Kentucky, Cumberland, and Ohio rivers. Cherokee headmen signed in mid-March; warrior Dragging Canoe opposed the sale and warned the country would become dark and bloody. Virginia later voided the private purchase but compensated the company with Ohio River acreage that seeded Henderson County.

properties.name: Bardstown Founding
properties.title: Bardstown Founding
properties.subtitle: Nelson County seat / Beech Fork
properties.history: The Bardstown area was explored in the mid-1770s and briefly called Salem. In 1780 William Bard surveyed a town on a 1,000-acre grant for his brother David and John Cockey Owings and set aside ground for public buildings. Named seat of new Nelson County in 1784, it was chartered by Virginia as Baird’s Town in 1788 and settled into the name Bardstown—one of Kentucky’s oldest inland towns.

properties.name: John Floyd / Floyd's Station
properties.title: John Floyd / Floyd's Station
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County / Beargrass Creek
properties.history: Virginia surveyor John Floyd led a 1774 Fincastle party into Kentucky, staked 2,000 acres on Beargrass Creek, and came back in 1779 to stockade Floyd's Station near today's St. Matthews. Virginia made him a Louisville trustee, Jefferson militia colonel, and in 1783 one of Kentucky's first two judges. On April 8 that year he rode toward Bullitt's Lick in a scarlet coat; a shot from ambush dropped him, and he died two days later at 32.

properties.name: Georgetown / Royal Spring
properties.title: Georgetown / Royal Spring
properties.subtitle: Scott County / Elijah Craig spring
properties.history: In July 1774 John Floyd claimed a thousand acres around a big Bluegrass spring. John McClelland built a cabin and stockade above it in 1775; an attack on December 29, 1776, killed McClelland, and the station emptied in 1777. Baptist preacher Elijah Craig later laid out Lebanon on the same spring, won a 1784 Virginia charter, and in 1790 renamed the place George Town for Washington. Scott County's seat still drinks from Royal Spring.

properties.name: Leestown
properties.title: Leestown
properties.subtitle: Franklin County / Kentucky River port
properties.history: In 1773 the McAfee company and Hancock Taylor surveyed a buffalo crossing on the Kentucky River about a mile north of today’s Frankfort. Hancock and Willis Lee planted a village on the north bank in 1775, the first Anglo-American settlement north of the river. Raids emptied it in 1777; it returned as a tobacco warehouse and shipping port for hemp, corn, and whiskey, and in 1827 limestone for the Old State House was quarried from the riverbank here.

properties.name: Squire Boone / Painted Stone / Long Run
properties.title: Squire Boone / Painted Stone / Long Run
properties.subtitle: Shelby & Jefferson counties / 1781 massacre
properties.history: Daniel's younger brother Squire Boone carved his name into a Clear Creek rock, painted the letters red, and by spring 1780 planted Shelby County's first large station about two miles north of present Shelbyville. After an April 1781 wound left Squire's right arm permanently short, most settlers fled toward Linn's Station and walked into the Long Run Massacre of September 13. He later rebuilt a mill on the burnt site before land debts cost him the station.

properties.name: Paris Founding
properties.title: Paris Founding
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County seat / 1789–1790
properties.history: Joseph Houston's 1776 station sat near Doyle Spring. Lawrence Protzman later platted 250 acres and in 1789 got Virginia to charter the town as Hopewell as Bourbon County's seat. In 1790 James Garrard and locals renamed it Paris to match the county, itself named for France's Bourbon kings who backed the Revolution. The post office briefly ran as Bourbonton before Paris stuck.

properties.name: Capt. Will Emery / Long Hunters
properties.title: Capt. Will Emery / Long Hunters
properties.subtitle: Warren County / hunting-ground conflict
properties.history: Shawnee held the larger northern and central Kentucky hunting grounds; Cherokee worked closer to Cumberland Gap. When long hunters stacked pelts for eastern markets, Native parties treated them as poachers. Around late 1769 a Shawnee band with Captain Will Emery took Boone and John Stewart’s six-month haul and warned them home: stay out, or the wasps and yellowjackets would sting. Not blank wilderness—a contested commons.

properties.name: Christopher Gist / Ohio Company
properties.title: Christopher Gist / Ohio Company
properties.subtitle: Fayette County / 1750–51 survey
properties.history: Fifteen-plus years before Boone’s fame, the Ohio Company hired surveyor Christopher Gist to probe the Ohio Valley down toward the Falls. Crossing into Kentucky from the Scioto mouth, his journal logged rich bottomlands, canebrakes, buffalo plains, and Native towns. Shawnee at Lower Shawneetown warned him off the Falls; he brought the company a fossil “beest” tooth from Big Bone country and the first detailed English read of northeastern Kentucky.

properties.name: Jacob Spears
properties.title: Jacob Spears
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County / early bourbon whiskey
properties.history: Pennsylvania-born Revolutionary veteran Jacob Spears settled near Paris in Bourbon County and was distilling by the 1790s. Thomas Metcalfe built his stone house (“Stone Castle”) around 1790; the farm still holds a springhouse and whiskey storehouse—Kentucky’s most complete early distiller’s complex. Spears floated barrels down the Licking to the Ohio and on to New Orleans, and he is often credited among the first to market the county’s whiskey under the name that stuck: bourbon.

properties.name: John Filson
properties.title: John Filson
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County / Filson Club pin
properties.history: Pennsylvania schoolteacher and surveyor John Filson reached Lexington around 1783 with land warrants for more than 12,000 acres. In 1784 he published The Discovery, Settlement and Present State of Kentucke—the first written history of the country—with a companion map engraved in Philadelphia. The book’s appendix carried the earliest printed Boone narrative; in 1788 Filson helped plat Losantiville (later Cincinnati) and that October vanished while surveying near the Great Miami.

properties.name: Lexington & Ohio Railroad
properties.title: Lexington & Ohio Railroad
properties.subtitle: Franklin County / first KY railroad
properties.history: On January 27, 1830, Kentucky chartered the Lexington & Ohio—the commonwealth’s first railroad, and among the first west of the Alleghenies—to tie Lexington to the Ohio River. Track used English strap iron spiked to quarried limestone sills; horses pulled early cars, then steam. The “Daniel Boone” engine made Lexington to Frankfort in about two and a half hours in 1835, cracking open Bluegrass freight toward the river long before the Civil War.

properties.name: Bland W. Ballard / Tyler Station
properties.title: Bland W. Ballard / Tyler Station
properties.subtitle: Shelby County / Tick Creek
properties.history: Born Spotsylvania County, Va., October 16, 1761, Bland Williams Ballard came to Kentucky in 1779 and scouted for George Rogers Clark. With Robert Tyler he helped plant Tyler Station on Tick Creek east of Shelbyville around 1781. In 1788 Delaware warriors killed his father and several siblings near the station; Ballard fought through Fallen Timbers, survived capture at Frenchtown, represented Shelby County in the General Assembly, and died September 5, 1853. Ballard County carries his name.

properties.name: Gaitskill Mound
properties.title: Gaitskill Mound
properties.subtitle: Montgomery County / Adena tablets
properties.history: On Mount Sterling’s northern bypass, Gaitskill Mound is an Adena earthwork (roughly 800 B.C.–A.D. 700) listed on the National Register in 1975. Unlike many looted mounds, it yielded rare engraved stone and clay tablets recovered through University of Kentucky work associated with W.S. Webb—ritual objects tied to Adena cremation and mound ceremony rather than everyday trash. The site anchors Montgomery County’s deep Woodland past beneath the later townscape.

properties.name: James C. Crow / Oscar Pepper
properties.title: James C. Crow / Oscar Pepper
properties.subtitle: Woodford County / Labrot & Graham ground
properties.history: Scottish physician-chemist James C. Crow began advising Oscar Pepper's Woodford County farm still on Glenn's Creek by 1833. After Pepper rebuilt in stone (1837–38), Crow returned as master distiller (1840–55), measuring mash temperatures, yeast, and acidity with scientific care that fixed sour-mash practice as commercial habit. His whiskey shipped far beyond Kentucky; Old Crow later took his name, and the limestone valley still hosts Woodford Reserve on the old Pepper ground.

properties.name: Isaac Shelby
properties.title: Isaac Shelby
properties.subtitle: Lincoln County / Traveler's Rest
properties.history: Maryland-born Isaac Shelby fought at Point Pleasant, then helped lead the Overmountain Men to victory at Kings Mountain in 1780. He moved to Kentucky in the 1780s, helped push statehood, and in 1792 became the commonwealth's first governor; sixteen years later he returned as fifth governor and led militia at the Battle of the Thames. Shelby County still carries his name, and Traveler's Rest marks his home ground.

properties.title: William Whitley / Sportsman's Hill
properties.subtitle: Lincoln County / Crab Orchard
properties.history: Near Crab Orchard, William Whitley finished Sportsman's Hill (1787–1794), often called Kentucky's first brick house—thick walls, elevated windows, and hiding places against raids. Beside it he ran a clay oval where horses raced counter-clockwise, a pointed break from English turf clockwise. The house and hill remain a Lincoln County historic site.

properties.name: Estill's Defeat
properties.title: Estill's Defeat
properties.subtitle: Montgomery County / Little Mountain 1782
properties.history: On March 22, 1782, Capt. James Estill and about 25 Lincoln County militiamen overtook a Wyandot raiding party at Little Mountain Creek, near today’s Mount Sterling. After nearly two hours of fighting, Lt. William Miller’s left flank broke, the Wyandots closed, and Estill was killed in hand-to-hand combat along with six of his men. The fight—also called the Battle of Little Mountain—was one of the bloodiest single engagements of Kentucky’s “Year of Blood.”

properties.name: Cumberland Gap / Thomas Walker
properties.title: Cumberland Gap / Thomas Walker
properties.subtitle: Bell County / geologic doorway
properties.history: In March 1750 Dr. Thomas Walker led a Loyal Land Company party through the Appalachians and on April 13 recorded Cave Gap: a plain Indian road, a spring pouring from a cave, marked trees, and a pass visible for miles. He named the gap and nearby river for the Duke of Cumberland and later had a small cabin raised near present Barbourville—the first Euro-American house claimed in Kentucky. Walker’s journal mapped the geologic doorway later generations would pour through.

properties.name: Catherine Spears Carpenter
properties.title: Catherine Spears Carpenter
properties.subtitle: Casey County / 1818 sour-mash recipes
properties.history: Twice-widowed Catherine Spears Carpenter ran a large Casey County farm after 1806, raising crops, livestock, and surplus corn into whiskey. County tax records show her paying on 100 gallons of spirits in 1815. An 1818 manuscript in the Carpenter Family Papers preserves sweet-mash and sour-mash distilling recipes she used to instruct her household—one of the earliest written American sour-mash records, decades before James Crow’s fame.

properties.name: Wickliffe Mounds
properties.title: Wickliffe Mounds
properties.subtitle: Ballard County / Mississippian town
properties.history: Mississippian farmers founded Wickliffe around AD 1100 on a bluff over the Ohio, three miles from the Mississippi confluence. They built platform mounds, a plaza, houses, and after 1175 a cemetery mound; by 1350 the community capped its mounds and left. In the 1930s a promoter opened graves to tourists as “Ancient Buried City”; Murray State later professionalized the research, and the site became a state historic site in 2004.

properties.name: Falls of the Ohio
properties.title: Falls of the Ohio
properties.subtitle: Clarksville / Jefferson fossil beds
properties.history: About 390 million years ago a shallow Devonian sea laid down the Jeffersonville Limestone—coral banks and stromatoporoid sponges now exposed at the Falls of the Ohio. Those hard shelves made the only major rapids on the river, so flatboats had to portage; Louisville and the Indiana towns grew at that choke point. George Rogers Clark staged from Corn Island in 1778. The beds have been a National Natural Landmark since 1966.

properties.name: Lower Shawneetown
properties.title: Lower Shawneetown
properties.subtitle: Greenup County / Scioto mouth KY bank
properties.history: Long before stations dotted the Bluegrass, a major Shawnee town straddled the Ohio at the Scioto’s mouth near today’s South Portsmouth. English maps called it Lower Shawneetown; by 1751 eyewitnesses put the population around 1,200. It was a diplomatic hub and western end of Pennsylvania’s southern deerskin trade until 1758, when the Shawnee moved north. Kentucky archaeology still holds Fort Ancient pottery mixed with mid-1700s trade goods from the Bentley and related sites on the Kentucky bank.

properties.name: Indian Knoll
properties.title: Indian Knoll
properties.subtitle: Late Archaic shell midden · Ohio County
properties.history: Five thousand years before the first stations, Late Archaic hunter-gatherers kept returning to a shell midden on the Green River in Ohio County. Indian Knoll (15OH2) yielded over a thousand burials, twenty-three dog burials, and more than 50,000 artifacts when University of Kentucky crews dug it in the late 1930s WPA years. In the early 1990s it and nineteen other Green River shell middens became National Historic Landmarks.

properties.title: Danville Constitution Square
properties.subtitle: Boyle County / statehood conventions
properties.history: After the Kentucky District court moved from Harrodsburg to Crow’s Station, Danville’s public square (laid out 1785) hosted ten conventions from 1784 to 1792. Delegates there framed the first state constitution in April 1792, clearing the way for Kentucky to enter the Union as the fifteenth state on June 1. Replicas of the log courthouse, jail, and meetinghouse still mark the ground.

properties.subtitle: Mason County / 15Ms1

properties.name: Indian Fort Mountain
properties.title: Indian Fort Mountain
properties.subtitle: Madison County / Berea Pinnacles
properties.history: On a knobby ridge south of Berea, dry-laid stone walls ring Indian Fort Mountain (15Ma25) in the Berea College Forest. Hopewell-era Middle Woodland people built them about 2,000 years ago as a hilltop enclosure, more a ceremonial marker than a stockade. Tests in 1980 treated the tumbled rock as linear mounds rather than a fighting wall. The site went on the National Register in 1983; hikers still climb the Pinnacles over the same ground.

properties.name: Ashland Central Park Adena Mounds
properties.title: Ashland Central Park Adena Mounds
properties.subtitle: Boyd County / Central Park
properties.history: Six conical Adena burial mounds still sit in Ashland’s Central Park, roughly 15–20 feet across and 4–6 feet high in a slight curve. UK archaeologists Webb and Funkhouser recorded them in 1932; a 1930s survey said no Kentucky city held more prehistoric evidence than Ashland, though many other local mounds were leveled for streets. Listed on the National Register in 1974, they mark Woodland mound-builder presence along the Ohio centuries before historic tribes.

properties.name: Mount Sterling Founding
properties.title: Mount Sterling Founding
properties.subtitle: Montgomery County seat / Little Mountain
properties.history: Explorers out of Boonesborough called a tree-covered Adena burial mound “the Little Mountain.” Scotsman Hugh Forbes began selling lots beside it around 1790; in 1792 the Kentucky Assembly chartered the town on 640 acres. Forbes meant Mount Stirling (for Stirling, Scotland, plus the mound); the misspelled “Sterling” stuck. The mound—once about 25 feet high at Queen and Locust—was leveled in 1845, and Mount Sterling became Montgomery County’s seat.

properties.name: Winchester Founding
properties.title: Winchester Founding
properties.subtitle: Clark County seat
properties.history: Clark County was carved from Fayette and Bourbon on December 6, 1792, and named for George Rogers Clark. Justices first met at John Strode’s station, then voted to put the public buildings on John Baker’s land by his spring. On December 17, 1793, the Assembly established a town there named Winchester, after Baker’s hometown in Frederick County, Virginia. A two-room log courthouse went up in 1794; Winchester remains Clark’s seat.

properties.name: Hardin Village Fort Ancient
properties.title: Hardin Village Fort Ancient
properties.subtitle: Greenup County / 15Gp22
properties.history: On the Ohio floodplain in Greenup County near South Shore, Hardin Village was a late Fort Ancient town occupied from the late 1500s into the early 1600s and covering more than ten acres. University of Kentucky digs in 1939 and again in the 2010s mapped large bark-walled houses, storage pits, and family cemeteries. Triangular endscrapers point to intensive hide work for long-distance exchange—marine shell and brass among the imports—just as the protohistoric Ohio Valley was tipping toward abandonment.

properties.title: Richmond Founding
properties.subtitle: Madison County / Miller's barn courthouse
properties.history: Madison County's first seat sat at hillside Milford with thin water. In 1798 the legislature let the court move onto Revolutionary War veteran Col. John Miller's land along Otter Creek; the county paid angry Milford residents before carting records to Miller's barn. On July 4, 1798, trustees named the new seat Richmond for Miller's Virginia birthplace, surveyed fifty acres into lots, and built a brick courthouse on the barn site in 1799. Richmond incorporated in 1809.

properties.name: Peter Village enclosure (15Fa166)
properties.title: Peter Village enclosure (15Fa166)
properties.subtitle: Fayette County · Early Woodland ditch-and-embankment · ~5th c. BCE
properties.history: North of Lexington in Fayette County, Peter Village (15Fa166) is a huge Early Woodland ditch-and-embankment enclosure—about 9.2 hectares, irregular rather than a neat geometric circle. Long mislabeled an Adena “village,” it is better read as a specialized gathering and craft place; archaeologist Berle Clay tied it to barite and galena working, and newer geoarchaeology (Henry and others) points to dual embankments and construction as early as the 5th century BCE—among the earliest monumental enclosures in the Middle Ohio Valley. It sits near the better-known Mount Horeb circle, marking Bluegrass ritual landscapes centuries before forts and stations.

Muir shows Bluegrass Fort Ancient life before the big nucleated towns.

properties.subtitle: Henry County · salt lick & early boiling works
properties.history: In Henry County, Jacob Drennon and Matthew Bracken claimed the big salt lick on July 26, 1773; Nicholas Cresswell in 1775 described some fifty acres of buffalo-trampled ground and springs strong enough to leave salt crusts in the sun. Virginia’s Patrick Henry patented 400 acres including the springs to George Rogers Clark in 1785, and boiling works rose that winter.

properties.name: Maj. Joseph Bowman
properties.title: Maj. Joseph Bowman
properties.subtitle: Clark’s second-in-command · Harrodsburg petition 1776 · died 1779
properties.history: Virginia-born Joseph Bowman came to Kentucky by 1775, signed the 1776 Harrodsburg county petition, and in 1778 raised a company for George Rogers Clark. As Clark’s second-in-command he took Prairie du Rocher, St. Philippe, and Cahokia after Kaskaskia fell, kept a day-by-day journal of the flooded winter march to Vincennes, and was promoted major just as a celebratory powder explosion burned him badly. He died at Fort Patrick Henry on about August 14–15, 1779 — the only American officer lost in the Illinois campaign.

properties.name: Owensboro / Yellow Banks
properties.title: Owensboro / Yellow Banks
properties.subtitle: Smeathers cabin 1797 · town 1816–1817
properties.history: Frontiersman William Smeathers (Bill Smothers) built a cabin on the south bank of the Ohio in 1797 at a landing flatboat men already called Yellow Banks for its clay bluffs. Daviess County was created in 1815; the town was laid out in 1816 and incorporated in 1817 as Owensborough for Col. Abraham Owen, killed at Tippecanoe in 1811 (the spelling shortened later). Smothers later scouted for Stephen F. Austin's Old Three Hundred in Texas. Downtown Smothers Park marks the home site — western Kentucky's river gate still sitting on that yellow bank.

The legislature recognized the town in 1809.

Digs recovered dense burials, hearths, mussels, fish, nuts, and Green River humped bannerstones—another node in Kentucky’s densest Archaic shell-midden landscape.

properties.name: Capt. Jack Jouett / Craig’s Creek
properties.title: Capt. Jack Jouett / Craig’s Creek
properties.subtitle: Midnight ride 1781 · in KY from 1782 · Woodford house 1797
properties.history: On the night of June 3–4, 1781, Capt. John “Jack” Jouett spotted Banastre Tarleton’s British cavalry near Cuckoo Tavern in Virginia and rode roughly forty miles over back roads to warn Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and the Virginia Assembly at Charlottesville. Most of the government escaped; Virginia rewarded him with a sword and pistols. By 1782 he had moved west into what became Kentucky, represented Lincoln/Mercer and later Woodford counties as a statehood backer, and in 1797 built a brick Federal house on a 530-acre Woodford farm near Craig’s Creek — still standing as the Jack Jouett House Historic Site.

properties.name: David Snowden homeplace
properties.title: David Snowden homeplace
properties.subtitle: Lee County · St. Helens · Middle Fork Kentucky River
properties.history: Historic Snowden homeplace near St. Helens (Lee County), on a knob by the Middle Fork Kentucky River (KY 52 east of Beattyville). David Snowden Sr. (1759 near Perth Amboy, N.J. – 1839 Estill Co.) served as a Revolutionary War frontier “Indian spy” and guard from Washington Co., Pa. (federal pension W9308), and also on Gen. Lachlan McIntosh’s 1778 Ohio campaign and Col. William Crawford’s 1782 Sandusky expedition; he married Nancy Hazelrigg in 1782. His son David Snowden Jr. (1786–1852) built a log cabin, kitchen, and quarters here about 1825; a later two-story clapboard house on sandstone had a wing that served as the St. Helens post office. The family also appears in Owsley County around 1850 before Lee County split. The abandoned house was photographed extensively and was reportedly demolished after a fire. Photos: https://abandonedonline.net/location/david-snowden-house/ and https://abandonedonline.net/david-snowden-jrs-house/ . Pension abstract: https://kygenweb.net/estill/military/revwar/snowden01.htm.

Their linsey-woolsey cloth became a frontier staple; she later ran an ordinary (tavern-inn) and is buried in the Fort Harrod Pioneer Cemetery (d. 1815).

properties.title: Henry McKenna
properties.subtitle: Fairfield · Nelson County · Old Line sour mash 1855–1883
properties.history: Irish immigrant Henry McKenna of County Derry settled at Fairfield in Nelson County, began distilling in a mill shed by 1855 (under a barrel a day), and built a brick distillery by 1883. He sold only "H. McKenna Old Line" sour mash—never green whisky under three years—and stamped barrels with an Irish harp. The brand later survived Prohibition as medicinal whisky; Heaven Hill revived it in the modern era.

properties.name: John Finley
properties.title: John Finley
properties.subtitle: Eskippakithiki trade ~1752 · Boone expedition guide 1769 · Clark County
properties.history: Long before Wilderness Road fame, Pennsylvania-born trader John Finley (also Findley) was crossing the Alleghenies for furs. Around 1752 he reached Eskippakithiki, the Shawnee town in today’s Clark County, one of the earliest recorded Euro-American trading trips into central Kentucky. Years later, as a Braddock-campaign acquaintance of Daniel Boone, he returned to the Yadkin with stories of cane-rich hunting grounds beyond Cumberland Gap. In May 1769 he guided Boone’s party through that gap; Finley’s firsthand routes—not Boone alone—helped open the country settlers would soon claim.

properties.title: Springfield / Washington County seat
properties.subtitle: First county after statehood 1792 · town laid out 1793 · Matthew Walton
properties.history: Washington County was the first county the new Kentucky legislature created after 1792 statehood, named for George Washington. In 1793 a site near the old Wilderness Trace was chosen for the seat on land tied to Gen. Matthew Walton; surveyor David Caldwell laid out the public square, and the town took the name Springfield. Early stations—Sandusky (1776), Cartwright’s (1778)—and Parker’s Landing on Beech Fork had already drawn settlers from the Gap road; Maryland Catholics arrived in force from 1785. The Lincoln family later settled nearby on Beech Fork, and Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks’s marriage bond still sits in the Washington County clerk’s office.

properties.name: Ruddell's Station
properties.title: Ruddell's Station
properties.subtitle: Harrison County · fort 1779 · Bird capture June 1780 · South Fork Licking
properties.history: In spring 1779 Capt. Isaac Ruddell rebuilt a fort on the South Fork of Licking (Harrison County) on the old Hinkson site—Ruddell’s Station, or Fort Liberty—soon joined by many Pennsylvania German families. In June 1780 British Capt. Henry Bird marched south with cannon, Canadian volunteers, and hundreds of Native allies. Artillery cracked the log walls; Ruddell surrendered under a promise of protection, then watched the agreement collapse as roughly four hundred captives were marched toward Detroit. Two of his sons were adopted by Shawnee; Stephen later lived as Tecumseh’s companion. The British never again brought that scale of artillery into Kentucky.

properties.history: In Shelby County, Isaac Watkins petitioned to lay out Simpsonville in 1816 as a waystation on the Louisville–Shelbyville road. A post office opened in 1821; the town incorporated in 1833. It was named for Capt. John Simpson, a Shelby County lawyer and Speaker of the Kentucky House (1810–11) who fought at Fallen Timbers (1794), won a seat in Congress in 1812, then died at the River Raisin on January 22, 1813. By the mid-1820s the place was a busy Midland Trail stage stop — home ground for anyone driving US 60 past Bagdad today.

properties.name: Tolu Site (15Cn1)
properties.title: Tolu Site (15Cn1)
properties.subtitle: Crittenden County · Mississippian · occupation ~1200–1300 CE
properties.history: Near Tolu in Crittenden County, the Tolu Site (15Cn1) was a Mississippian town occupied mainly about 1200–1300 CE (pottery styles; occupation into the 1400s). It once held three mounds — a platform, a burial mound, and a third of unclear use — and belongs to the Angel phase “Kincaid Set” with Angel (IN), Kincaid (IL), and Wickliffe (KY). Webb and Funkhouser excavated it in 1930; a 1954 plow find west of town produced one of the finest Mississippian fluorite statues known, complete with a rare beaded forelock.

properties.name: Saltpeter Cave (Carter Caves)
properties.title: Saltpeter Cave (Carter Caves)
properties.subtitle: Carter County · War of 1812 niter mining · 15Cr99
properties.history: In Carter County’s Carter Caves State Resort Park, Saltpeter Cave (15Cr99) was mined for potassium nitrate during the War of 1812, when British blockades forced Americans to scrape gunpowder ingredients from their own caves. University of Kentucky archaeologists in the early 1990s documented impressions and remnants of 26 wooden leaching vats — a hybrid of big-box and small V-shaped cottage setups with wooden piping. Kentucky caves yielded more than 300,000 pounds of saltpeter statewide; this one is on the National Register and open for summer tours.

properties.name: Jenny Wiley / Big Sandy
properties.title: Jenny Wiley / Big Sandy
properties.subtitle: Captivity & escape 1789–1790 · Johnson Co. settlement 1800
properties.history: On October 1, 1789, at Walker's Creek in present-day Bland County, Virginia, a Cherokee–Shawnee party seeking revenge on Matthias Harman mistakenly hit Thomas Wiley's cabin. Jenny (Virginia Sellards) Wiley saw her brother and three children killed; she and an infant were taken captive. Over nearly eleven months in the Big Sandy country the infant died and another child born in captivity was killed. She escaped by following a dream-path of creeks to Harman's Station near present-day Paintsville, where men built a log raft and pulled her across. Reunited with Thomas in Virginia, the couple settled on Tom's Creek in what became Johnson County in 1800; she died there in 1831. Jenny Wiley State Resort Park on Dewey Lake near Prestonsburg carries her name.

properties.name: Buckner Site (15Bb12)
properties.title: Buckner Site (15Bb12)
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County · Fort Ancient occupation ~1200–1550 CE
properties.history: Near Paris in Bourbon County, the Buckner Site (15Bb12) holds two circular Fort Ancient villages around central plazas, occupied mainly about A.D. 1200–1400 and into the early 1500s. Wall-trench houses, shell- and limestone-tempered pottery, triangular points, and a stone-paved McCray Mound mortuary area show maize farmers tied into Ohio Valley exchange. University of Kentucky WPA crews dug there in 1939; later work mapped the rings. It was listed on the National Register in 1983 (address restricted) — Bluegrass country that was already a settled farming landscape centuries before Paris or Bourbon whiskey.
